speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Implementing lifelong learning will require more than expanding opportunities for adult learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Lifelong learning will push systems to fundamentally rethink the timing and sequencing of education and skills development over an individual's life course.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This includes the early stages of learning from childhood and into early adulthood and beyond.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Learning trajectories will become more complex for people of all ages, requiring more sophisticated support arrangements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Establishing how individuals learn best at different stages in their lives and how to distribute learning opportunities and resources over the life cycle will become key policy paradigms.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We have done much over the past years in building and fortifying our education system to help ensure that each and every student has an opportunity to the provision of multiple pathways offered by our education system.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Moving ahead, the challenge falls on how to marry, match the passions and interests and aspirations of every Singaporean and to help every Singaporean to realise fully their true potential.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To ensure our education system continues to be future-ready and future-proof, I opine that that should be greatest synergy, collaboration, linkages and integration between the mainstream education, pre-employment training all through to adult and worker continuing education training and learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In short, the entire continuum and ecosystem needs to rethink what we teach, when we teach, where we teach and how we teach.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to better align the future of education and learning to the future of work and workplaces.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is crucial if you want to truly embrace the love of learning and lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The old adage of "learn, work and retire" will become passé.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If I may draw on some learnings of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) report on the future of education.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Tomorrow's educational institutions will need to help learners to think for themselves and join others in work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Educators will need to learn to learn learners develop a strong sense of right and wrong and a sensitivity to the claims that others make.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Individuals will need to learn to live with themselves, with others and with the planet.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At work, at home and in the community, people will need a deep understanding of how others think, whether as scientists or artists, and how others live in different cultures and traditions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Technology is also creating new, alternative channels for human learning outside of institutional frameworks.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Isolated time and space for learning was necessary when teachers and resources were scarce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But the ubiquity of opportunities will allow learning to move beyond its institutional confinements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Technology can support both learning throughout life as well as ways to recognise such learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Moving learning out of its institutional and age-related barriers will create important public policy challenges, requiring the development of new partnerships, support learning with innovative arrangements on both the supply and demand side.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Teachers in our schools and educators in our Institutes of Higher Learning, including in the PEIs and CET centres, have undergone much change and have had to grapple with the many exacting requirements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In a similar vein, the future of teaching is fraught with new challenges.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The age old one-size-fits-all teaching method has long been outgrown, with the focus moving on to catering teaching methods to different styles of learners.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Classroom management and curriculum will also need to keep pace with changes across industries, including a need to foster a global mindset in today's students.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To keep pace and stay abreast of what is happening across industries and sectors, I suggest that MOE allow our teachers and adult educators an opportunity to take sabbaticals and industry attachments, including secondments outside of MOE and the private sector for an extended period of time so that they can translate their learnings, experiences in their teachings, when they return to the education space.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For our students, classrooms would continue to move towards being paperless and more computer based.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Though the students will incorporate much independence into their learning process, mentoring will become fundamental to our student and learner success.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As such, more resources should be dedicated by MOE to this function, which actually integrates leading with early career guidance, which I submit, we can do more of and better in across the board.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to promote more equal distribution of training opportunities for workers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore’s education system, as we know it, will lose its currency and relevance if we do not make some important moves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are enough evidence and inputs to inform us on what the future of education will look like.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Traditional content such as basic literacy, English, Mathematics, will need to be updated; adding to them, digital literacy, data literacy, financial literacy and a slew of competencies, attributes and values needed to survive in this age of unprecedented change.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Person-centred, competency-based, mastery-based, self-driven, bite-sized, just-in-time, chasing skills, not paper; classrooms without walls, schools without walls – these are all quoted as the future of education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Members of this House have just seen the National Library Board’s latest blueprint that talks about learning marketplaces, learning superstores that serve all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And NLB is not even part of MOE.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, update and cascade the vision of education so that more Singaporeans are aligned in our end in mind, from K to 12, from young to old.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I fully resonate with Education Minister Chan Chun Sing’s views of what education should be – of continual learning, connecting, collaborations and confidence building.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Makes a lot of sense, if we think of how every Singaporean ought to prepare for each of the average four to five job changes he makes in his working life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, address the restraining forces of change, the often unspoken elephants in the room.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The glaring and valid concern of educators in the face of an ever increasingly overloaded curricula; an expectation of the educators to pivot to become content curators, learning designers and life coaches; and then to teach in a way that they themselves had not quite experienced before.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What about the less glaring but stronger restraining force that is unseen, below the waterline?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The beliefs, the conditioned behaviours and fears of the very people involved in education: our school leaders, educators, parents and employers?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Someone once quipped that education is an inherently conservative social enterprise and changing education systems is sometimes like trying to move a graveyard.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We are so used, for example, to use the academic yardstick in parenting, in hiring and even in judging each other.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Pick a few strategic pilots and go for broke.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore will not be the first in the world to operate through-trained Primary to Secondary schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore is blessed to have a teaching workforce that is well regarded, professional and motivated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Their mothership, the National Institute of Education, will need to be prepared to raise our educators to find their place in the new enlarged education ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: NIE will have to rethink its traditional modes of management, collaborate and connect with local and global partners, to reframe and to refresh its institution and offerings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Lastly, let us start addressing the challenges of adult learners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are of course challenges – not availability of courses only but likely the motivation to learn or the way by which adult learning is designed and offered.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But focus, we must, seriously on our adult and older learners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If we do not, many of them will become Singapore’s future low-wage earners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Think big, believe big and let us act now.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, Marva Delores Collins, an American educator who is famed for her teaching method and for her work in educating impoverished students once said that “when someone is taught the joy of learning, it becomes a lifelong process that never stops, a process that creates a logical individual.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is the challenge and joy of teaching.” Although this adage was made years ago prior to the advent of the Internet and before the age of technology assisted learning, it is now truer than ever.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In today’s day and age where new knowledge is constantly being created and new skills render old ones irrelevant, it is important for educators to inculcate the joy of learning in students so that they are truly educated and have learned how to learn, not just schooled.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we know the importance of inculcating the joy of learning in students, it is a challenge to do so in an assessment-driven and exams- focused education system where rote learning and regurgitation might reap great rewards.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe this was a step in the right direction, I commend MOE for this, as it encouraged students to uncover the joys of learning without having to worry about how well they do in summative assessments like exams.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Without a doubt, summative assessments are still important because they allow us to assess how much the students have absorbed the material and knowledge, and tests and exams are useful indicators of one’s progress in knowledge acquisition.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But, as I have said before in this House, formative assessments can also provide an indication of a student’s development and academic growth.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Grades can also be apportioned to coursework and there are many subjects that are based on 100% coursework.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many parents and students alike heaved a sigh of relief as they were uncertain of the requirements due to the disruptive nature of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Exams do add a huge amount of stress to students.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Frequently, students spend hours trying to memorise the content of the textbooks which they had studied during the year in order to regurgitate the answers to which their teachers want to read in the student’s exam script.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But in today’s world, knowledge content, while it is still important, is no longer the sole criterion of a person’s ability.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Dean designate of the new NUS College, Prof Simon Chesterman, wrote an Opinion article for The Straits Times in January this year.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In his article, he shared that in the past, “teachers and professors were in possession of knowledge, and they were paid by students, or their parents, or the state, to pass on that knowledge to the students.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, today, every student holds a device that can access almost all of human knowledge.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, our phones are a portal to vastly more knowledge than will ever fit into any of our brains.” In view of the availability of technology, I urge MOE to review the current curriculum of the students.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Instead, more focus can be placed on how the student can do research or acquire information; how to discern truth from false information.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is the training of the mind to learn how to acquire knowledge that is more important.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can MOE also emphasise on the overall development of a student’s character so that the student can be prepared for life ahead in the real world?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Education should be a journey where a student enjoys and takes delight in learning and the discovery of new things which are important to him in life.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It should not be a stressful period because of the need to memorise school work and to pass year-end examinations.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Chairman, I have two kids who are in Primary school.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Parents all want the best for our children, and we may have different ideas of what is "best", and have different levels of means to provide.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Some people send their children for enrichment classes, some assign their kids chores at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Whatever method is used, there’s generally more awareness now to teach life skills and resilience.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: There have been many positive changes in our formal education since when I was in primary school.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: There is more structured learning, and improved communications with parents.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: There are great resources on the MOE website on social and emotional learning.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But theory is just the beginning, the challenge is in the real life implementation.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I want to register my thanks and appreciation for school teachers and educators of all levels, who have been working doubly hard in these COVID times, to provide face-to-face lessons, and to also standby for home-based learning, in addition to doing safe distancing measurements.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I am thankful to them for keeping such a close eye on our children.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Parental involvement is essential to a child’s educational journey, but I have to constantly remind myself not to solve every problem for them.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I have met older teenagers holding part-time jobs and doing their part to pay for their schooling.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I have also met people in their 40s, who still need to ask their parents for all decisions, because that is how it has been their whole lives – to check with their parents.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Personally, I see that my role as a mother is to provide for them and to teach them to be the best they can be.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This may start from the playground, to allow them to climb and fall- while we stand ready to catch them, rather than forbid them to climb at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, that any delay would simply mean that students go to bed even later and, second, that such delays could give rise to disruptive rush-hour crunches.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first assertion, as it turns out, is one that is weakly supported by evidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many credible studies have shown that affording adolescents additional sleep can have yielded payoffs in terms of improved behaviour, health and academic outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is even so, with a relatively modest delay of just half an hour or so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, the reality is that students are already experiencing sleep deprivations from the status quo.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Think of all the marginal steps that parents take – the additional hours of supplemental tuition, the move to a neighbourhood closer to a preferred school, the endless bottles of essence of chicken.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And it strikes me as failing to pick the lowest hanging fruit when we look at more expensive and intrusive educational interventions but neglect this relatively simple one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As for the second assertion, I am sure that we will all agree that we should not be compromising as important an outcome as student performance simply in favour of one of logistical convenience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I am not suggesting any strict guidelines for post-Secondary levels, it is reasonable that ITEs, Polytechnics and Junior Colleges start even later, at 9.00 am.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The additional half hour for upper-Primary students is consistent with how sleep phase delay may occur as early as the onset of puberty and also, certainly, by the time that they are teenagers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And since Primary cohorts are also comparatively larger than Secondary cohorts, it also makes sense to balance out the inflow of students headed to schools in the morning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While delays for upper Primary and Secondary school students will, undeniably, alter traffic patterns, its contribution to the overall morning rush-hour jam is likely to be somewhat limited.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The half-hour delay for half the Primary cohort would likely add a limited number of additional vehicles to the road, seeing that many upper Primary school students would already begin travelling to school by public or private buses by then.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, these buses would, in any case, begin their pick-up rounds between 7.00 am and 8.00 am, well before typical work start times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And as more Secondary school students already know how to travel to school independently by public transportation, their even later start time will also likely have a limited impact on traffic patterns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, with more parents working from home or exercising flexible work schedules in a post-pandemic world, it could easily be the case that any anticipated increase in rush-hour traffic be offset by the reduction in working commuters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The staggered school start times could also carry a tangential logistical benefit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Schools currently often face jams during arrival and dismissal times, with roads surrounding schools ensnarled by traffic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is an isolated but genuine problem as those of us who have received complaints from residents living near schools would well understand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Staggering school start times could reduce the incoming traffic by as much as a third, which would help alleviate this morning school rush-hour crunch.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, first of all, I declare that I run an education company operating education centres and a private school.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Members of Parliament across time and political parties – Ms Paulin Straughan, Mr Hri Kumar, Mr Yee Jenn Jong, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, Mr Kok Heng Leun, Ms Denise Phua and myself – have spoken up either for the scrapping of PSLE or a through-train pilot programme giving parents and students the option of bypassing PSLE.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSLE remains the most stressful examination for local parents and students.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Despite changes to the assessment, the PSLE stakes are high for parents, educators and students.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chronic stress from high-stakes examinations on young children is undesirable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Neuroscience tells us that long-term negative stress impedes the brain development of children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are bad outcomes for their esteem and mental health.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lately, tragic incidents have given us a rude wake-up call to pay more attention to the mental well-being of our students.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, efforts have been made to reduce stress on students by removing examinations at certain levels.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the PSLE is the elephant in the room.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A previous Education Minister has said that “removing the PSLE and having a through-train will only transfer the stress on parents and students elsewhere, such as at the P1 registration”.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if the through-train programme is implemented in a limited number of schools while the mainstream is still on the PSLE system, this would not happen.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would, at least, give parents and students a choice.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we learn from the experience, we can decide later whether the through-train programme should be extended to more schools.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Today, I wish to again urge MOE to consider implementing a pilot project of a through-train programme.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Members from different parties have urged the Government to scrap PSLE and allow parents and students to bypass PSLE.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSLE remains the most stressful examination for local parents and their children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chronic stress from high-stakes examinations form a long-term negative stress that can impede the brain development of children and also affect children's esteem and mental health.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lately, tragic incidents have given us a wake-up call to pay more attention to the mental well-being of our students.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A previous Education Minister has said that "removing the PSLE and having a through-train will only transfer the stress on parents and students elsewhere, such as at P1 registration".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if the through-train programme is implemented in a limited number of schools, while the mainstream is still on the PSLE system, this will not happen.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will at least give parents and students a choice.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we learn from the experience, we can then decide whether we should extend it to more schools.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): In 2020, MOE announced the introduction of student-initiated learning (SIL) in Secondary schools, Junior Colleges and MI.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, if there are schools that have implemented SIL last year, how was it implemented and what was the outcome?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can MOE confirm that no students are without access to PLD due to financial reasons?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After one year of implementation, how has PLD affected the students’ learning?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It was deemed necessary for madrasah students to meet this benchmark to ensure that they will be able to complete their Primary education and will possess the minimum academic standards required for them to qualify for Secondary school.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Aside from that, all madrasahs have been able to meet MOE’s benchmark.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the PSLE results of madrasah students in the past two years have been extremely encouraging.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Through the efforts of the madrasah administrators and teachers and support from both MUIS and MOE, madrasahs have become private educational institutions that provide quality education to its students.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A madrasah that cannot take in new students may find it difficult to continue operating as a private education institution.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: When MOE announced this new arrangement, it was to provide students with a more customised learning experience according to their subject-specific strengths and interests and to empower students to take greater ownership of their learning.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Have we been able to quantify and qualify the benefits enjoyed by the students?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Although I hope that is not the main indicator of the performance of the programme, I would like to ask the Minister what is the proportion of students who have been able to move to a more demanding level?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I would also like to ask about the experience of teachers, Allied Educators and executive and administrative staff of the schools in running SBB.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Unfortunately, SBB started around the same time as the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: With students being grouped in different classes for different subjects, this might prove challenging when we are trying to minimise interactions in a school.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I am aware that providing a safe learning environment is already taking a toll on everyone in school.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I hope that our school staff well-being is also taken into consideration when SBB is being piloted and rolled out.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: With these learnings, are we in good stead to progressively roll out SBB to more Secondary schools this year?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I welcome this move as it will do much to remove the stigmatisation of being in a less academically demanding stream.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: More importantly, it recognises and reminds us that each of us has different strengths, even among various academic subjects.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Unfortunately, this means that more residents are speaking less of their mother tongue at home.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our ability to be bilingual or trilingual gives us a huge advantage when it comes to competing for jobs locally, regionally, globally, and this makes us an attractive business hub.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Having a strong command of our mother tongue is not only important culturally, but also economically, if we want to stay relevant and remain ahead in the global competitive market.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, I would like to ask the Ministry if there are any initiatives that students can get to expand their opportunities to learn about their mother tongue languages and culture, beyond exams.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, similar to Member Denise Phua, I agree with Minister Chan Chun Sing's speech on the three Cs that our universities should achieve: continual learning, connections and collaboration for value creation, and confidence building.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And certainly, learning must not stop at a tertiary level.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we track and monitor progress, both at the individual learner level and also at the societal level?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What measurables do we use to define whether someone is a lifelong learner?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These days we try to avoid labels, but it is still important to have some tangible ways to determine whether the various programmes are effective.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to help promote lifelong learning in our youth and prepare them for the new challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What does this mean for IHLs in shells in terms of delivery of content and certification?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the past, students were largely graded based on how they performed on paper.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Assessments have since evolved over the years, with internships, project work, exchange programmes and 360° evaluations counting to their graduation results, but COVID-19 has nevertheless disrupted in-person learning and training.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will IHLs work with industry players to enhance the learning process for our students?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For most students, the hands-on work experience with industry stakeholders will be their first taste of formal working experience, so it should be a meaningful and enriching one.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we encourage more on-the-job training (OJTs) with industry players?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, are there other societies and countries that we are studying with regards to the best practises for continuous learning?

speaker: Mr Chairman
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Choosing the best course they can get into, based on "cut-off points, study hard, get good grades, get a job".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is the Government doing to encourage young Singaporeans to explore opportunities and embrace the lifelong learning mindset from a young age, even while they are still in the formal education system.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, taking part in boot camps outside of the university curriculum or during NS.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Governments need to move away from the idea that they can educate and prepare our workforce of X number of graduates for the labour market, that has led to their configuration of schools, universities, polytechnics, ITEs and other institutions that we know today.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Learning would include specific technical skills demanded by industry, but also digital skills, life skills, and as we work towards a greener future, sustainability skills.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can the Government encourage our IHLs to strengthen partnership with industries and develop these ecosystems, in order to better serve their evolving role in higher education and continual learning?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I would like to declare that I am an advisor to the National Instructors and Coaches Association, an association formed by the NTUC.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As CCAs are essential to students holistic education through the discovery and development of talents, interests, characters and values, our MOE instructors and coaches play a significant role in this aspect.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Throughout this pandemic, MOE instructors and coaches who experienced difficulties in conducting CCAs in schools, COVID-19 uncertainties surfaced the issues of pay-per-use contracting model.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This was a result of discussions between MOE and National Instructors and Coaches Association (NICA) last year.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: NICA appreciates MOE's intervention, especially given a time when MOE had to implement various learning modes due to the evolving COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: NICA hopes to foster this dialogue and partnership further with the common goal of providing high-quality CCAs for the holistic development of our students.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a result, some instructors and coaches may win multiple contracts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For those with too many contracts, they are forced to withdraw their bids.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Often, this creates a delay in CCA start date, as affected schools then have to issue new Invitations to Quote (ITQs) with a later award.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This affects students’ CCA learning outcomes and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This ensures that MOE instructors and coaches are able to design and execute structured programmes based on the development runway for NSG or SYF which often takes more than a year to train for.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this way, students can be assured of learning with a clear structured runway.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The curriculum created and proposed by the instructors and coaches should be the intellectual property owned by them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Being a key stakeholder in the education ecosystem, instructors and coaches are nurturing partners that can be counted to support schools, teachers, and students.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through this partnership, I believe our children will benefit from a balanced and well-rounded education that is aligned to MOE’s mission.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Chairman, a strong education system is built around a few key pillars, one of which is to have passionate educators who are committed to bring out the best in every learner.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Educators who not only teach textbook knowledge but also bring with them different perspectives and experiences that can enhance the learning of our learners.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I believe that our MOE educators are committed professionals who have been given very good preparatory training that equipped them with the academic and pedagogical development knowledge, as well as with classroom management skills before they are deployed to teach in our schools.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: That said, that continuous professional development is very important, especially in the area of pastoral skills.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Today, teachers not only have to deliver and teach, Chairman, they also have to manage the emotional and mental well-being of students and deal with interactions with parents, which are likely to be outside regular classroom hours.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: These are chronic stressors that might negatively impact the mental well-being of teachers, especially sustained over a prolonged period.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Another area where I hope MOE can consider is how to enrich the learning experience of our students, by encouraging educators with more diverse backgrounds to join the profession, or to ensure that our educators have diverse exposures, so that they can bring additional perspectives to the curriculum that they teach.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Many educators went straight into the teaching service from NIE out of a passion for wanting to educate young minds and to serve the community through education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: So, could MOE please share if there are such plans for the professional and holistic development and training of our educators?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Chairman, I began my career as a teacher more than 20 years ago, and have taught at various levels from Primary to Secondary schools, Polytechnics and University.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Like many of my fellow educators, what keeps us going is our love for teaching.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The joy of curating lessons and imparting knowledge to students is hard to describe.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: But being an educator it not just about teaching.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The inconvenient truth is, educators wear many hats.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: They are administrators, disciplinarians, confidantes, counsellors, peer support advisors, CCA coaches and managers, amongst others.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: And certain hats require them to work beyond their work hours.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: In my recent Budget speech, I mentioned about the need for individuals to undergo phases to re-invent themselves, to prevent them from going through physical and mental burnouts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: I also believe that it is important to expose educators to new and different opportunities beyond their teaching scope.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: And this includes the deployment and workload as well as defining clear working hours and discourage educators from responding to emails and texts so that they are well rested mentally and physically.

speaker: Mr Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, you can take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my Budget speech last year, I called for a performance management system or stack-ranking to be more standardised, transparent, fair and informative for teachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have done a lot for our students, we stopped ranking them and comparing them to their peers during PSLE, we tell them learning is not a competition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why then do we make teaching a competition?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It seems contradictory that teachers are the ones telling students that students are no longer ranked and compared with their peers when they themselves are ranked and compared with other teachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOE has bee engaging teachers on improving the performance management systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like our students, our teachers deserve a nurturing environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Teachers wear many hats from teaching the curriculum, to holistic development, CCAs, and now COVID-19 regulations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We keep adding to teachers’ workload, but we still expect the same quality output from them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The working hours have increased over the pandemic and our overstretched teachers are reaching out for help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Teachers shared with me that they are stressed and overworked.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One shared, "Many teachers are burning out, but seeking help is not an option because we are expected to show up for our students.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I’ve had multiple anxiety attacks in school but I have to put up a front to go back to class." Will MOE consider setting limits for teachers’ working hours and workload?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Other than enhancing the Parents Gateway, reducing coverage of national exams, removing some school-based exams, how else will MOE reduce teachers’ workloads?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like many of us, teachers should enjoy flexible work arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They prepare and send their children to school every morning before rushing to their own school.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a parent myself, I experience this chaos every morning.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some teachers struggled with this, including my resident who told me that her principal does not allow her to have staggered working hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the other hand, I know of teachers who do and I used to take the elevator every morning with a teacher who sends his child to school before going to his school late.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should ensure consistency across schools and all teachers should have FWAs, including staggered working hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another teacher shared with me about flexible working hours for teachers without children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She shared that her school allowed her to leave school after 11.30 am if there are no matters in school.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, another school only allow teachers to leave after 2.30 pm even if they have classes before that.

speaker: Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A carefully curated learning experience will enable students to better understand local and regional culture, traditions, work ethics, people and history.

speaker: Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must also ensure that sufficient amount of time is spent in the region to enable one to form an assessment and better understanding of the region, develop useful engagements and relationships that would enable them to build up familiarity and courage to further engage the region in the future.

speaker: Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How is the Ministry strengthening the diversity of experiences to better understand culture, people and history of the region?

speaker: Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How can we give everyone an opportunity to have a immersive overseas experience?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I wanted to find out the extent to which students from well-off families were concentrated in the more popular and well resourced group of schools.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I unsuccessfully attempted to file a follow-up question this January asking if MOE possesses this data.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The question was not allowed on grounds of repetition.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2018, Prime Minister Lee acknowledged the fears of popular schools becoming closed circles.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Note that I am asking for data on SES by category of schools and not by each individual school.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: We need to strengthen the support for mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: We need more early warning capabilities to identify students who need support and to be able to provide these capabilities much earlier.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: As mental well-being cuts across various domains, we must be able to coordinate our approach together with other stakeholders and parents.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: We must be able to respond appropriately with a range of responses and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: How are we building up capabilities to build conducive and supportive environments for higher ends students?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: How are we assuring that we are nurturing students with special needs today and equip them with skills for life?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, former Manpower Minister Mr Lim Swee Say once mentioned should Singapore be hit by higher employment, it would be because of a shortage of skills as a result of the widening of job skills mismatch – and not a lack of jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How is our education system preparing our students for employment in the skills-based economy?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the digital nature of all jobs now, how do we ensure all our students leave our education system with skills to perform at least tech-light roles?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we consider coding, dashboarding or data visualisation as a core skillset for our students to acquire before they leave Secondary schools?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Chairman, there are many ways for an admission to the Polytechnics.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Apart from the Joint Admission Exercise (JAE), there is also the Early Admissions Exercise (EAE) for graduating "O" level students, who receive conditional offers based on their aptitudes and interests before taking their GCE "O" levels.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The Direct Admissions Exercise (DAE) allows applicants who are not eligible to participate in the EAE and JAE to apply for the course of their interest.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: And finally, there is the Polytechnic Foundation Programme (PFP), a one-year programme that accepts Normal (Academic) students.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: I have witnessed many students from the PFP programme as well as those from the ITEs, and they are doing just as well as or even better than their "O" level counterparts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: We can do more to continue to change mindsets and show that truly, there are multiple paths to success.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: There are several questions that I would like to raise.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Second, for students enrolling in Polytechnics from the ITEs, are there plans to introduce industry attachments prior to this admission so that they are better prepared before they embark in the diploma programme?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: And finally, for students who need more time to build up their academic foundation, what are some of the options for them to be eligible to enrol in Polytechnic courses based on their non-academic achievements?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It was found to be "comparable to pre-COVID-19 levels".

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And if that is available, what are the employment rates and starting salaries?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Has it improved over the year, or rebounded to pre-COVID-19 levels?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: What is the percentage of ITE graduates who have furthered their studies instead?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I understand there are many traineeships available currently for these young graduates.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, may I know the rate of conversion to full-time employment for the ITE graduates and if they are comparable to those from Polytechnics and Universities?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For those who have been unable to convert, what are the reasons cited by the ITE graduates as well as the companies themselves?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Should there be initiatives to encourage companies to hire ITE graduates?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is of concern to me as if these graduates are not able to get decent-paying full-time employment, many of them might turn to gig work, especially if they have to help with their family finances.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The longer they stay in gig work, the more difficult it will be for them to get out.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, my focus on Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) is more towards both Institute of Technical Education and Polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Our country education landscape and system of IHLs had evolved over the past few decades since I last completed my Diploma in 1992 from Singapore Polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I am very heartened to see the increase and Improvement not just for Polytechnics, but even in converting them – from Vocational Institute of Training Board to one that is more encouraging: Institute of Technical Education, in short ITE.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Since this change, can MOE share how many students have graduated yearly and how fast do they actually get employment?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I also note that there are many ITE students that choose to continue to acquire Diploma upon graduation before entering their work life.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Can MOE share how many students have gone through prior this route after taking the Higher Nitec straightaway into Diploma?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Aside from ITE, the number of Polytechnics has increased gradually from two to five now.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Can MOE share how many graduates annually from such Polytechnic across the five different ones?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding, the thing that is more of concern is how are the courses curated so that it can meet the industry demands?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: How often are these courses reviewed and even new courses curated, to meet potential demands of the future job market?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Does MOE also work closely with EDB to ensure that we have sufficient required talents to meet the future economy and industry demand so that we can build a Singaporean Core in our workforce and also provide good global job opportunities?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, I also call MOE to work closely with NTUC via our young NTUC team so that these students can have a teaser on work-life and from then on learn the need for continuous learning in their future career.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, I would like to declare my interest as CEO of WMI, a continuing education and training (CET) provider.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Much has been said about the rapid pace of industry development and how jobs are fast evolving.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This means the acquisition of new skills and knowledge must keep pace and even intensify over our lifetime.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is timely that we think about how CET can be even more impactful and emerge as a strategic pillar in our human capital development.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What about the contribution we should expect from employers?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: One of the struggles we often hear from working adults is that it is already hard enough to cope with the day’s work, let alone set aside time to learn new skills.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: CET can take place in different ways, both online and offline, on campus as well as at the workplace.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can we support workers, integrate Continuing Education and Training to their work, including the provision of study leave as part of employment terms?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The credentials from CET must translate to job opportunities and career growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For this to happen, there must be close partnerships among CET providers, employers and the industry to agree on industry accreditation standards and the recognition of a common set of CET qualifications.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Mr Chairman, education and personal development is indeed a lifelong journey.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: This axiom is now more apt than ever.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The Fourth Industrial Revolution or Industry 4.0 was coined by Klaus Schwab, the founder and executive chairman of the World Economic Forum in 2016 to describe how the confluence of artificial intelligence, advanced robotics, Internet of Things, quantum computing, genetic engineering and other technologies will create the perfect storm that paves the way for radical transformative changes in the conduct of businesses and how we live our lives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Today, we are barely five years from that and into the Industry 4.0 and futurists and academics have already begun to describe how the Fifth Industrial Revolution, Industry 5.0, will look like.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: As one consulting group has aptly described, Industry 5.0 is the new renaissance for humanity where humanism, civility, inclusivity, creativity and purpose will thrive alongside profit and digitally enabled progress.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Singapore needs to prepare our workforce for Industry 5.0 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Our educational institutions have traditionally focused on Pre-Employment Training (PET) to prepare our young for work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Compared to a few years ago, it is now becoming even clearer that getting a basic education is a necessary but insufficient condition for work in Industry 5.0 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: We need to develop a new educational framework that integrates PET with Continuing Education and Training (CET) to meet the new reality of work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Chairman, MOE has traditionally focused on PET and CET has typically been the domain of SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) and Workforce Singapore (WSG).

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Moving forward, would we see a closer integration between the PET and CET frameworks so we can develop a future-ready workforce that is equipped with basic know-hows as well as the mindset that training and development is a lifelong journey, especially in Industry 5.0 and beyond?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: How could MOE, SSG and WSG work together to re-conceptualise how the education landscape will look like in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Being relevant to the industry is of utmost importance to strengthen employability and continued employment.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Mid-career upgrades and continued learning is not an easy feat as one usually has to manage multiple obligations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: I know of many who will take time after a long day of work to attend classes or courses.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: We have a duty of care to them.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: We must make sure that their efforts will be accretive to their careers and to their personal development.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The Government has invested resources, manpower and funds into the sector and many of us are grateful.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There are three compelling reasons why it is time for SPED schools to be elevated, to be uplifted to be more prepared for the future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: One is the incredulous pace at which technology has changed lives at home, at work and out in the community.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: We need a breakthrough in the SPED education system for higher returns in the form of physical wellness, literacy, numeracy, community living and independent living skills as a result of a SPED education career.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Three, the need to continue learning for life and throughout life is even more critical and urgent for students with special needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: SPED school graduands literally stop learning after they leave the school gate.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: In a complex, rapidly digital, volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous (VUCA) world, the Government must facilitate the transit of SPED schools to become better schools for the future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: One, SPED schools of the future must be scoped to cover lifelong learning – to learn for life and to learn throughout life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Special education can no longer be about frontloading content in the first 18 years of one's life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Learning must extend beyond 18 to avoid the falling off the cliff with no hope of any more education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Two, SPED schools of the future must be masters of their mission.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: No lip service to SPED basics like person-centred planning, individual education planning and other aspects of disability-specific curriculum, pedagogy and assessment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: SPED schools must become truly schools without walls and strongly facilitate learning at home, in the community, at the workplace and care facilities – just in time, self-paced and appropriately paced, bite-sized, with repositories of learning resources which are easily accessible.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Three, SPED schools of the future must develop strong thought leadership and practice to the extent that it can guide and inform the support of students with special education needs (SEN) in mainstream schools – in MOE schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: In education systems elsewhere, educators with strong expertise in SPED are better regarded and even better paid.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Singapore has only begun its journey in building expertise in special education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: To reach this leadership position, the National Institute of Education, NIE, the mothership that now trains special educators, will need to upgrade and update its current service model.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Four, SPED schools of the future should be led not just by MOE but by a SPED Leadership Council at the national level comprising many strong helping hands, with members who can represent the ecosystem of SPED – the Government, disability and education experts, family representatives and the industry.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: SPED schools of the future should be trusted.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: They should not be managed in a cookie-cutter way.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: They should be trusted to deliver according to the outcomes agreed upon.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: SPED schools of the future should not be micromanaged and those who are competent and have a proven track record should be given more autonomy and space to innovate, to experiment and to break new grounds, just as how MOE has allowed for the autonomy of schools and IHLs in the mainstream.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Lastly, SPED schools of the future must actively partner and enskill family caregivers in the education of their students, of their children.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Parents or caregivers will play an active role in the education of their own children.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: They will not wait till when they or their children become much older to worry about their unpreparedness for life or life after the parents' death.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Parents of children with special needs face a complex dilemma when making educational choices for their children.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A wide range of services is available at various price points but parents are largely left on their own to identify the optimal ones.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Could ECDA provide more one-stop advisory services for parents?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will help ease the anxiety that many parents of special needs children feel.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For children who require medium to high levels of early intervention support, such services can be prohibitively expensive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A centralised provision of early intervention services can bring economies of scale which can reduce costs for parents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Children who require lower levels of early intervention support can attend mainstream Primary schools but may still require supplemental support services like occupational therapy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can MOE provide an integrated special needs support programme at mainstream schools?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will enable children with special needs to thrive in such environments and reduce the cost and inconvenience borne parents for external support services.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Like other parents, parents of children with special needs like me also want to see our children do well in school and achieve their fullest potential.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The education journey, though, is often a lot more challenging.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The children are differently abled and require more support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If we intervene early in schools and give them the necessary skills to prepare them for the future, there is a greater chance that many of them could carry on with their lives with minimal reliance on others and work and socialise like everyone else.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If they can be independent and contribute meaningfully towards the economy, less resources need to be spent on support structures or schemes when they are adults or when they age.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is thus important to have the appropriate educational pathways for these students to prepare them well so that they can integrate and contribute to society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Schools offer the support structure for parents in their children's developmental journey.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The challenge for parents sometimes is in getting to the services they need, in enrolling in appropriate schools which are within the vicinity of their homes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Special Education (SPED) schools play a key function in the special needs community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How can we continue to enhance the accessibility and affordability of SPED schools?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is also particularly challenging for families as their children move on to different stages of their developments.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should continue to build on the efforts to support special needs students as they transit into the various milestones in their lives.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Chairman, last year, we were rocked by the unfortunate loss of life in school during school hours.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The incident impacted many – students, educators and parents.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Inevitably but most unfortunately, the issue of mental health was brought to light.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Our educators are trained to look out for signs of distress amongst their students and mental well-being is taught in the curriculum.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: There is also a peer support programme to bridge the gap.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: However, as an educator and a peer support coordinator, I find that it is not easy to identify these students.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: I have had students coming up to me and sharing their difficulties and I in turn, in confidence, make subtle arrangements to accommodate such students.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: But often, they go totally unnoticed or students and parents are aware but would like to keep their issues private.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Over the past two years, I have asked for mental health literacy programmes, screening both physical and mental as well as time-outs to be introduced.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: I am grateful that Character Citizenship Education (CCE) now covers the literacy aspect and I hope that the Ministry can integrate screening as well as time-outs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chairman, we thank Members for their suggestions and the support for our education system and especially our educators.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Let us also thank our educators on the frontline.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: COVID-19 has accelerated many trends and heightened the need to evolve our education system urgently.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Ms Denise Phua also spoke about the future trends of education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We aim to emerge stronger from this pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will not waste the opportunities that have arisen from this crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will lock in the gains from the disruptions to distinguish ourselves for the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chair, three driving forces shape our education system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, technology and business cycles have become more compressed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Workers now take on multiple jobs in their lifetime and need to be reskilled regularly to remain relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How fast we evolve our skills, products and services will determine our competitive advantage, both as individuals and as a nation, much more than our population base or our resources.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, the world is becoming polarised and fragmented, even as we grow more inter-connected and inter-dependent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Competition of ideas and values, contestation of ideologies and influence.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Countries that cannot create relevance for themselves will have to worry about having to choose sides.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Yet, there are opportunities for those that can value-add and play the role of a connector to transcend these fault lines.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our people have more diverse aspirations and perspectives.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Internet has increased access to information but algorithms on social media can also skew the information that we are exposed to.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They cater to our preferences and amplify our biases.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our youths are not just Singaporeans, but also digital natives.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Technology and social media have allowed them to stay connected and organise around meaningful causes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But it is also easier to compare themselves with their classmates and friends, as well as anyone else in the world online.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This has an impact on their sense of identity and self-confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have seen other societies with longer histories fracture, as the values and aspirations of their people diverge.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The definition of success for our education system must then evolve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It must enable every Singaporean to do justice to their own set of gifts; constantly seeking to surpass themselves both individually and as a team, rather than just surpassing others; contributing towards a better future for the wider community, to Singapore and to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Confidence starts from understanding our own strengths and interests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Then, confidence comes from knowing that we have multiple pathways that give our people lifelong opportunities to acquire the knowledge and skills for success through life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must also have confidence in our values and solutions, that we have the will and the means to chart our own destiny with our own solutions for our own context.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This comes from our speed of evolution and our superior connectivity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Evolution speed depends on us quickly learning, unlearning and relearning, so that we can combine and recombine ideas and knowledge to always create something new and relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Superior connectivity enables us to go beyond geography and size, with the world as our hinterland and market.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As the world threatens to fragment, we connect and value add.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This connectivity is our special, man-made competitive advantage.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We distinguish ourselves as a nation that celebrates our diverse roots while forging a shared identity with a set of shared values.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We begin by giving every child a good start in life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The early years set the foundation for heathy and balanced development for our children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As they progress through our schools, we build on these fundamentals by giving our students greater confidence in themselves and of their abilities, with more opportunities to explore their interests and cultivate their curiosity, so that they are unafraid to try.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And if they fail, they pick themselves up and try again.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We cannot shield our children from all uncertainties and the imperfections of this world, nor should that be our aim.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But we certainly can and want to equip them with the skills to manage the uncertainties and navigate the imperfections.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This means creating time and space for our students to develop the life skills they need for success, including the ability to deal with failure, inventive thinking, adaptability and cross-cultural skills that Mr Darryl David and Mr Lim Biow Chuan raised.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Over the past few years, we removed mid-year examinations for Primary 3, Primary 5, Secondary 1 and Secondary 3.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Schools and teachers can better pace and deepen students’ learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They use ongoing assessments to identify what students have mastered and the areas they have difficulties with.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This frees up more time across all levels for self-directed learning and development of 21st Century Competencies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are also reviewing curriculum content and assessment demand.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Any one standard curriculum will necessarily not be able to meet the diverse learning needs of our students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Any "average curriculum" will necessarily mean that many students will be overstretched while others are under-stretched.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Hence, we must have a range of options to cater to our students' diverse abilities and learning needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our teachers must have the ability to pick and choose from a menu of options and customise them to suit the diverse and respective needs of their students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These moves seek to bring about a cultural shift: where our students learn holistically and master skills, driven by intrinsic motivation and future relevance, and not be distracted by incessant comparison with others.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chair, next, we want to customise education as much as possible to bring out the best in every child.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will give students more agency in their learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This lets students take ownership of their learning at their own pace.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Students will also have dedicated time and space to pursue their own interests outside the curriculum through Student-Initiated Learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And we are studying how technology can further customise learning to help teachers provide feedback, track students’ learning progress, and we will also explore the use of adaptive learning systems to tailor learning to our students’ needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We thank Ms Denise Phua and Ms Hazel Poa for suggesting a through-train system for Primary to Secondary school education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ms Denise Phua has raised this idea for some time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The PSLE remains a useful checkpoint for our students and parents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We made significant changes to the PSLE scoring system last year, to broaden emphasis beyond academic results.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to look at ways to enhance the diversity of our school landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But there are some fundamental principles we must always maintain: to provide quality and holistic education for every child, no matter their learning profile; to give opportunities for children of different backgrounds to mix with one another to strengthen our social cohesion; and to ensure equity and fairness in admissions and posting.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng has asked for an update.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In the pilot schools, students taking different courses come together in mixed form classes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They take six subjects at the common level, which is one-third of curriculum time and other subjects at different levels.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The experiences from the pilot gives us confidence that we are on the right track.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Students have made more friends across courses, learnt new perspectives and learnt how to relate better to their peers from different backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And they have become more confident in themselves and of their abilities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In Secondary schools, students will be grouped in mixed form classes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Students can choose to take different subjects at different subject levels, suited to their pace of learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These subject levels, known as G for General: G1, G2 and G3.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They are broadly mapped from today’s Express, Normal (Academic) and Normal (Technical) standards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
