text: We are working with Government agencies, social media and technology companies and SSAs to create awareness of positive ways to use digital technology, harness technology platforms to promote a healthy online peer support culture and find practical solutions that mitigate online risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MOE is also part of whole-of-society efforts like the Youth Mental Well-being Network, which was set up in February 2020 by MSF, MOH and MOE to co-create ground-up solutions to improve youths’ mental well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary and Minister of State Alvin Tan will be announcing some updates on the Network later.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I have shared about our work with parents, Government agencies and the community to build an inter-connected network of care, support and opportunities for our students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Dr Mohamad Maliki had also spoken about our efforts, as part of UPLIFT, to build a strong network of community partners to support our disadvantaged students and their families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Minister Chan Chun Sing has shared about our partnerships with industry to provide more workplace learning opportunities for IHL students, and with Government agencies and companies to strengthen the employability and career prospects of our Polytechnic and ITE graduates in the future economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Together, these partnerships reflect our concerted, whole-of-society effort to transform the education system and achieve our vision of a confident, competitive and cohesive Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In Mandarin):   Our students face a future that is being shaped by rapid technological changes, a world that is increasingly polarised and fragmented, and a society with more and more diverse perspectives, ideas and values.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To respond to the opportunities presented by these forces of change, we must be prepared to continuously learn and relearn, transcend fault lines in the world, and stay cohesive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Beyond school, we have an entire ecosystem of continual education and training, which will move beyond training some thirty to forty thousand students every year to ‘retooling’ some three to four hundred thousand workers a year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This life course approach requires a whole-of-society effort.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Educators, parents, the community and industry partners are our essential partners in this endeavour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Let us journey together to strengthen our education system and achieve our vision of a confident, competitive and cohesive Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The second question is on the removal of mid-year exams for Primary and Secondary schools, which is upcoming.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Does it also mean that in the mid-year, there will not be any sit-down tests as well as weighted assessments?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, it is not just a one-time survey.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We regularly monitor this and we have a certain baseline to see whether there are specific areas that we should be concerned with, not just in general for the whole teaching population, but also, very specifically, whether any particular schools or any particular group of educators might be facing a bit more stress than others.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is the assurance that we can give Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, when I first went to MOE, I asked my colleagues: what is the difference between an exam and a test or assessment?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I learnt this new word and I understand what my professionals are doing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we will continue to have year-end exams where relevant and then we will couple that with continuous assessments module-by-module.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Some time ago, I made a speech where I did not suggest that we should remove the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: But rather, while we have PSLE, to also incorporate some coursework component such that every Primary 6 student ends up with an actual composite grade that is a combination of the PSLE examination and the coursework component that they have done, maybe a 70% examination, 30% coursework.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: So, I just wanted to ask the Minister if the Ministry is considering this and, if so, could he provide some thoughts on this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I mentioned earlier that I am really happy about the quality of our teachers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: But I also talked about the possibility of encouraging or having more mid-career teachers coming in from other jobs, other industries, into the teaching profession to bring their experience with them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: This can also be synced in quite nicely with continuing education and making sure that our people are trained to move into a different career.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Could the Minister perhaps update or share if the Ministry has any plans to enhance this or to have this as a more structured programme for mid-career switchers to come into the teaching profession?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Chairman, with your permission, if I may take the second question first and then I will come back to the first question, which I will give a more elaborate reply.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On Mr Darryl David's suggestion on having more mid-career teachers, indeed, we have a healthy pipeline of teachers who join us mid-career.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Every week, I visit at least one or two schools and every time when I visit the schools, I will always ask about their prior experience.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And just from my random sampling, I can see that we have a very healthy pipeline of people who are mid-careerists and decided to join the teaching service.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As Mr Darryl David says, they do bring with them a wide spectrum of prior experiences that they can share with their fellow teachers and also the students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having said that, I think we need it to be both ways, meaning that we need to recruit a fair share of mid-career teachers to enrich our portfolio of teaching experiences; at the same time, we must also enable our existing teachers in service to go out and build new connections and also to refresh themselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As I have always mentioned, I have never seen any of my teachers who were afraid of hard work, but instead, I think, when they work hard, they want to feel that they themselves are growing, that they also have the development opportunities so that they can feel refreshed, they can feel recharged and, if they feel refreshed and recharged, then I am very confident they will continue to spread this spirit of lifelong learning, the spirit of inquiry to their students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we will continue to do that, both ways, to have more mid-career people coming into service and also to have more people in-service going out to have exposure.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And this is particularly important for our Polytechnic and ITE lecturers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Chairman, on the first question of PSLE, I must share what is on my mind.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have given this very serious thought and I have listened very carefully to what Ms Denise Phua had said over the years.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The fundamental issue is this: why are our exams stressful?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have given a lot of thought about it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I will perhaps sum it up in these four dimensions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We then have to ask ourselves: why do we test?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And what do we do with the test results?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we are not clear on our answers to these four questions, then exams will always be stressful, never mind if it is PSLE or year-end exams.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we see a test or an assessment as an opportunity for us to know ourselves better, to know our children better – where they stand, where they are strong at, where they are weak at – then this self-assessment should not be stressful.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is about surpassing ourselves rather than surpassing other people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But if we get this wrong, if the reason for testing is to compare with other people, on a relative scale, then, by definition, any test will be stressful.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the test is to sort people out according to their different abilities, with serious consequences for their career pathways, then it will be stressful.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the first point I want to make is this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want to do away with this incessant comparison on a relative scale to truly appreciate what the child is strong in and what the child may be weak at and we need to help the child with.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think many Members have spoken on this and we agree.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Instead, going forward, it will be about how our children can apply the concepts they have learnt to solve tomorrow's problems.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Coming from NTUC and MTI, I can speak on behalf of the employers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All progressive employers are less and less interested in how our students are able to solve yesterday's problems with yesterday's solution or even today's problems with yesterday's solutions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All our progressive employers are looking for our students to be able to solve tomorrow's problems with tomorrow's solutions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Which means that more and more of our tests must be geared towards helping our students to prepare, to apply their knowledge in solving tomorrow's problems in context.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That does not mean that the tests will get easier.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, some people will think that tests by rote memory is easier.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But that is not the skillset that we are looking for, as many Members have said.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, with Google and the Internet, anyone can go onto the Internet to search for the information they require.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The new skillset that is required is how we make sense of the plethora of information and combine them and create new solutions in context.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Whether that is more or less stressful, it depends on our perspective again.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we test too early, as many Members have said, then it might be detrimental to some of the late bloomers, it might be detrimental to some of our younger children.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But on the other hand, if we test too late, we will be unable to apply the interventions necessary to help our children to progress at a pace that is suitable to them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, somewhere in between testing too early and testing too late, we need to find the Goldilocks point that is just right.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I must qualify, given the diversity of our learners, it is very hard to say that there is just one point for everyone.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But to the extent that we can, we will find that point – be it PSLE or otherwise – to cater to the bulk of our students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The final question is, what do we do with the test results?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not about going to a particular school that is deemed as most popular or most successful.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, having said this, I am under no illusion that exams will have some stress.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I must also qualify that it is not our aim to remove all stress from our children.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not possible and that should not be our aim.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having said that, we as parents, we as educators, we need to focus on these four sets of issues and hopefully find the correct answers for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Why we test, how we test, when we test and what do we do with the test results.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: One for Education Minister and the other for Minister of State Gan Siow Huang.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister to elaborate exactly how funding for CET will be enhanced to allow workers to attain a more substantial qualification that is relevant to their work.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, more investment: how exactly do we see that being evolved over time?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The second question is for Minister of State Gan Siow Huang.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Minister of State spoke a lot about career conversions programmes: place-and-train, train-and-place.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: And I do agree that these have been very useful for those whose career is in a transition.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: But I would like to ask about the framework that MOE is thinking for those who are still employed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, they are not in transition, they are still employed, that is the majority of the people.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: These are the people who would like to pursue CET, to develop mastery as well as updating their skills and knowledge about constant upgrade.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, how can we ensure the CET programmes are duly certified and recognised by the employers, as well as ensure that CET credentials are recognised within the industry to allow mobility across employers in the same sector?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I will attempt to take both of them.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: You would have noticed that SCTP is actually quite different from the past CET programmes that we had under SSG.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: You would notice that it is more holistic, it goes from the beginning to the end.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The beginning portion we will put in a skills advisory, training advisory type of discussion with the trainee so that the trainee can pick suitable courses, not just what he or she likes to do, but what we think might help the person get a job and also meet the person's aspirations.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I think that upfront is actually quite important.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The second thing about the SCTP is industry involvement, and that requires us to work with industries and some funding will be required for us to be able to scale this up.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And the third, the career coaching element and employment facilitation services, these are also very substantial investments that we are putting in.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, it is not a CET as in just training alone.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: But also translating it into getting jobs, good jobs for the individuals.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We have learnt a lot from this SGUnited Jobs and Skills journey.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We have learnt that individuals on their own, when they pick courses, the courses may not lead them to where they want to go.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Also, early career coaching, helping them discover their career goals and providing the facilitation can make a big difference in helping a person land a better job.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The second point about career conversion, indeed, there are many people, while they are already employed, are thinking of how to upskill, what to train themselves in, how to make themselves employable for a much longer term in their lifetime.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I would say that, over time, we have also taken on board a lot of feedback from individuals, as well as from companies on what would be useful, what mode of training would be useful.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: You would have noticed that now, there are a lot more bite-sized modules provided by our IHLs and our training providers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Some are online, some offline, all to tailor to the needs of busy working adults who want to upskill themselves but may not have the complete time flexibility to be able to do so consistently.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It is important that we build in a wide range of types of courses, different modalities and have a lot of flexibility for individuals to be able to choose courses, not just in terms of content that suits their needs, but the form of delivery.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: On the recognition of this type of training, we are undertaking a holistic review of our skills frameworks.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And in fact, we are working closely with our colleagues in MTI and MOM to make sure that the training investment, the courses, that we provide to Singaporeans, while the courses will be recognised not just by the institutions and training providers, but actually more importantly by the industries, by the employees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Just one point of clarification to the Minister Dr Maliki who addressed my cut and it is in relation to my cut where I asked if the Government can publish data by SES, background, for admissions into the different categories of schools: Government, Government-aided and Independent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think that having some transparency about that would be helpful to help us to monitor our progress to ensure that the more popular and well-resourced schools do not become closed communities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And that is the goal I think we all share.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would hope that the Government would consider just making that data public.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I just want to start off by saying that we understand that what he is saying is we should have a good mix of students to encourage social mixing, students from different backgrounds in our schools.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We must begin with the premise that no one education setting fits all students, although we have the same objectives in mind.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Our Independent schools, including Specialised Independent schools, there is some variation from the national average by virtue of the performance of the students at the PSLE – I mentioned during the Parliamentary Question by Mr Louis Ng earlier that there is a correlation between socio-economic background and performance at PSLE.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: But Independent schools cater to specific learner profiles that are different and with different aptitudes.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: But really, our fundamental objective is not to achieve identical profiles for every school.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Even our neighbourhood schools, they are identical in broad based curriculum, but they are unique in some specific aspects and because of that, almost all Secondary schools, in fact, all Secondary schools today, admit students in Secondary 1 through DSAs.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Which means that they are able to niche themselves sufficiently.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: DSA means that people with different unique talents go into the school.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: We want to encourage that diversity in our school systems and in our school environment.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, in the Independent schools, for example, we provide that opportunity for students from different backgrounds to interact.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, there is a good spread of students from different socio-economic backgrounds in all our schools, including our Independent schools.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Mr Leon Perera talked about how they are well-resourced.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I want to assure Mr Leon Perera that all our schools are well-resourced.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: In fact, in my speech, I spoke about resourcing schools with higher needs.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Because they have higher needs, we want to give the students the best that they could get and we respond to their needs accordingly.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: But even if we do see situations where schools may not have the demographic profile that reflects the national profile, we also encourage them to use other platforms for integration, for students to interact and appreciate the Singapore society's profile.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: For example, once the students are in school, we facilitate interactions like Values in Action projects not just within the school but across schools, projects, co-curricular activities (CCAs), joint CCAs, joint camps, cohort level camps – many opportunities for the students to interact.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, while the school provides certain experience which are relevant, with a right understanding of the objectives, it does not mean that our students are not interacting, that they are not mingling with students from different socio-economic backgrounds.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Integrated Programme (IP) schools are doing this too.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: For example, Anglo-Chinese School (Independent) works with Queensway Secondary School on their programme called the Play Inclusive Programme; Raffles Institution working with Crest Secondary School, collaborating with students in Scouts in the CCA, doing projects, community projects together; Raffles' Girls School with Edgefield Secondary School, with Guangyang Secondary School, collaborating on CCA programmes.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: So, it does not mean that we need to just focus ourselves on the profile of students in those particular schools when, as I mentioned earlier, in almost all our schools, the profile is generally reflective of the socio-economic backgrounds across our students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first builds on the question by Member Patrick Tay about abolishing the mid-year examination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Could I just clarify that the weight that was originally to be assigned to the mid-year will actually go to continuous assessment instead?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Because if not, of course, removing the mid-year just means that the final exam becomes even higher stakes and it is more stressful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Related to this, has the Ministry considered actually lowering the weight on this so-called synoptic assessment?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The second question is just to clarify what the Minister also said earlier on the later school start times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: He mentioned that there were many other schools with later starts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: How many schools or what proportion of schools have these later starts for at least the majority of the school days?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Chairman, the answer to Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's first question is that the weights in different schools differ slightly because of the different profiles of students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you would like to know the specific weights for different schools, then I think we can provide him with the information.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But as I have mentioned, the school profiles are all different and we should not try to homogenise, have a one-size-fit-all measure or yardstick to judge all our students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are moving towards a system that is much more customised to the respective needs of the students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second point, in fact, a lot of our schools have different start times.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some of them have later start times on certain days of the week but it all depends on when they start, when they end.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some of our schools have kept certain afternoons totally free for their students and their teachers to recharge and do other things.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we recognise that the learning needs of our students are diverse, if we recognise that the background profiles of our students are diverse, we should strive towards a system that provides more diverse options for our schools, our teachers and our students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think we must take care to not try to homogenise all the conditions when we in fact have agreed that we need greater diversity, which was what I mentioned in my speech.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I have gotten feedback from different schools on when they want to start and also when they want to end, which the day they want to start later and how much later.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, this is a very good exercise for our students and teachers to come together and decide collectively what are their priorities and how do they prioritise the time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will be very careful as the Minister for Education to try to dictate for every school, given their different conditions, to have the same start or end time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think I want my teachers, I want my students to have that agency to take charge of this and come to a reasonable understanding of where they want to be, given their different conditions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Can you keep it short and the responses can be short as well?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: My question revolves around the mental well-being of the students and teachers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Can the Ministry consider that as part of my clarification?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Number two is really on the students —

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Is it practical to have a hard cap?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am actually very heartened by the answers given to me by my teachers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We all know our teachers work way beyond what we expect of them in taking care of our children.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, for some of the high needs students, our teachers have no cap whatsoever.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Sometimes, they get into trouble with their families.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Sometimes, they get kicked out of their home in the middle of the night.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Many teachers in Northlight School gave their personal handphone number to their students to call them if they ever get into trouble outside school or if they ever got kicked out of their home.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have teachers that responded in the middle of the night, way past midnight, to pick up a student, to take care of them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, Mr Chairman, I think we all appreciate the point that we want to take care of our teachers and we want to do more.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And even if I do, I do not think my teachers will stop just because they consciously calculate that, "My time is up and therefore, I will not respond to this high-needs student of mine".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I think it is also not realistic for us to therefore say that every teacher shall not work more than x hours.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because their conditions are different, the types of students they are managing are different and I have seen all my teachers, including the very good teachers and counsellors in Northlight School, going way beyond their call of duty in order to take care of all our children.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: A big thank you to him as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: And the entire MOE team for giving us a good sharing of solving tomorrow's challenges with tomorrow's solutions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: On that final note, a big thank you to all our teachers and educators, past, present and incoming, for building this love for learning and embracing lifelong learning so that each and every one of us can stay future-ready, future-proof and be ready with new skills relevant to the new jobs and resilient for the future.

speaker: The Chairman
text: As Members would realise, normally as Speaker, I do not get to speak until the COS is over.

speaker: The Chairman
text: But I would have to make an exception at this moment, especially after MOE’s presentation on lifelong learning and continuing training and education, this feels like one such moment.

speaker: The Chairman
text: And you do not have to use your SkillsFuture credits for it.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am sure Members are all very passionate about the respective topics, a lot of clarifications to ask.

speaker: The Chairman
text: But I am sure the many Members would also understand how the process works.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Earlier, Members would realise there was a Point of Order called by Mr Leong Mun Wai, as he had some clarifications to be made.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There was also still discussion last week about tea break time and guillotine time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I understand and I was made aware that Mr Leong Mun Wai had also posted on Facebook.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I would not repeat everything, but he made a comment about “I have a number of clarifications to make but the Speaker didn’t even give me the chance.” And also, he added, “completely ridiculous.” I am sure Members understand how the process works.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am not here to speculate the intent and purpose of various Members’ postings.

speaker: The Chairman
text: But I thought it was opportune for me to refresh everyone’s memories about how this ought to work and why.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I believe we also do have reminders sent out to all our you.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will just repeat that: “I wish to remind Members that the guillotine time for Head X is such and such a time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The guillotine times are published for Members for information.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Members can file a Parliamentary Question (PQ) should they have further queries for the Ministry and should they be unable to raise their queries when the debate had ended." Let me go to the source, just to repeat.

speaker: The Chairman
text: If the time so fixed is reached before the head concerned is disposed of, the Chairman shall forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of that head.” Essentially, we have a time allocated for clarifications and there is a guillotine time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We work that out on a schedule basis and we will update on a daily basis.

speaker: The Chairman
text: And you are made aware of that time, so that we can continue to proceed with other orders of business.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I think it is important for us to understand that, and especially for the public as to how this works.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I know many of you would like to ask clarifications.

speaker: The Chairman
text: If any of you text me, grumbling about why, how come you have important question to ask and you cannot ask, I hope you bear with me for that.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It is important for us to understand this, because this is made clear to all of you and I am sure all of you understand that.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Just to also explain that when clarification time is reached and we have not reached guillotine time, then, it is the Chairman’s discretion as to whether we continue or not.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In the earlier debate, for example, with MOM, we had finished the clarification time and we continued all the way until guillotine time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am actually eating into your tea time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: As you will soon realise, your tea break will be a lot shorter than the 20 minutes allocated.

speaker: The Chairman
text: That is how we work out the various timings.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Another point to add, just so that you understand the thinking behind how I for example, call on various Members, I would like to give opportunities for various Members from various parties to be able to speak.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Different Members have opportunities to speak at other times.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, we would like to give that airtime to different Members as well.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I keep track of it because I write everything down and I try to roughly allocate that across the space of the whole COS and Budget.

speaker: The Chairman
text: And this includes, during normal PQ and supplementary question considerations as well.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, let me just remind everyone in case we forgot who we called in the earlier MOM COS debate, just for your own understanding.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I called Mr Desmond Choo, I called Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Louis Chua, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Abdul Samad, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, Leader of the Opposition Pritam Singh and Mr Sharael Taha, who wrapped it up.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have a number of Members who had asked to speak, such as Mr Edward Chia, Ms Janet Ang, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Leong Mun Wai, Mr Melvin Yong, Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Mr Leon Perera – and I apologise.

text: We did not have time because we reached the guillotine time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, I thought as a matter of record, it would be useful to just state this.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I would not pretend or do I wish to speculate as to why comments are made.

speaker: The Chairman
text: But I thought this might be useful to remind all Members of how the process works.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Unfortunately, as I said, the guillotine time for MOE, as you would realise, is 1630 hours.

speaker: The Chairman
text: And as a result of this clarification, I would now ask to take a break and take the seat at 4.30 pm.
